questions.q: Which constitutional provision forms the philosophical basis for India's neighbourhood policy, and what are its four specific directives?
questions.a: Article 51 of the Constitution (Directive Principles of State Policy) directs the State to: (a) promote international peace and security, (b) maintain just and honourable relations between nations, (c) foster respect for international law and treaty obligations, (d) encourage settlement of international disputes by arbitration. A wrong answer (e.g., citing Article 370 or Fundamental Rights) reveals confusion between justiciable rights and non-justiciable guiding principles for state conduct.

questions.q: Explain why the Gujral Doctrine (1996) was a significant departure from Nehru's non-alignment in managing neighbourhood relations, despite both emphasising peace.
questions.a: Nehru's non-alignment was a global Cold War strategy avoiding military blocs; the Gujral Doctrine is a regional policy of unilateral accommodation: India gives concessions to smaller neighbours without expecting reciprocity, respecting their sovereignty, non-interference, and peaceful dispute resolution. A wrong answer conflating the two shows inability to distinguish global strategic autonomy from regional hegemony management — a critical board exam differentiator.

questions.q: A student argues: "SAARC has failed because India dominates it; if India steps back, SAARC will succeed." Using the unanimity principle and two bilateral disputes, evaluate this claim.
questions.a: The claim oversimplifies. SAARC Charter requires unanimity for all decisions — any member can veto. Pakistan has blocked connectivity projects (e.g., SAARC Motor Vehicles Agreement) citing Kashmir; India blocked summit attendance after 2016 Uri attack. But India also initiated SAARC Satellite (2017) and COVID-19 Emergency Fund (2020). Failure stems from structural veto power + bilateral distrust, not just Indian dominance. Wrong answer ignoring unanimity rule misses the institutional design flaw.

questions.q: Compare the Indus Waters Treaty (1960) with the Teesta water-sharing stalemate (India-Bangladesh). What does the contrast reveal about the durability of water treaties when third-party mediation is absent?
questions.a: Indus Waters Treaty: World Bank mediated, survived three wars, has permanent commission and dispute resolution mechanism (Neutral Expert, Court of Arbitration). Teesta: No third-party guarantor, requires West Bengal's consent (Indian federalism), stalled since 2011. Reveals that durable transboundary water agreements need external enforcement mechanisms and insulation from domestic sub-national politics — a pattern seen in Mekong and Nile basins too.

questions.q: Assess the effectiveness of India's "Neighbourhood First" policy (2014–present) in achieving its stated goals of connectivity, development partnership, and security cooperation. Use two successes and two persistent failures.
questions.a: Successes: Bangladesh Land Boundary Agreement (2015), cross-border rail/power links, COVID vaccine diplomacy (Vaccine Maitri). Failures: Nepal's 2015 blockade perception and 2020 map dispute (Kalapani), Sri Lanka's Hambantota port lease to China despite Indian offers. Effectiveness is high on transactional connectivity, low on political trust-building where historical grievances and Chinese strategic inroads intersect. A purely positive or negative assessment ignores this sectoral variation.

questions.q: Draft a modified SAARC Charter clause that could overcome the unanimity deadlock while preserving sovereignty of smaller states. Justify each change.
questions.a: Proposed clause: "Decisions on economic cooperation (trade, energy, connectivity) shall be adopted by a two-thirds majority including India and at least three other members; political/security issues retain unanimity." Justification: Economic issues are positive-sum; political disputes are zero-sum. Two-thirds majority prevents unilateral dominance while allowing progress. Smaller states retain veto on sovereignty issues. A poor answer proposes majority voting on all issues, ignoring neighbours' fear of Indian majoritarianism.
